Federal money by program, compared

School meals and the SNAP connection

USDA pays districts for every meal served, at a free, reduced-price or paid rate. Under the Community Eligibility Provision (CEP), a school serves everyone free and claims a share of meals at the free rate equal to its identified-student percentage (ISP) × 1.6, mostly students matched to SNAP. Other schools claim students who qualify through SNAP matching or a family application. Either way, fewer SNAP households means fewer meals reimbursed at the free rate.

Spending by function, compared

Shading compares districts within each column (stronger blue = higher). Debt and construction swing with bond programs; recapture is what property-wealthy districts pay the state under Texas school finance.

Recapture ("Robin Hood")

Texas caps how much local property tax a district can keep per student. Property-wealthy districts send the excess to the state (recapture, under Chapter 49 of the Education Code), and the state puts it into the Foundation School Fund, which pays state aid to every district. TEA's books show exactly what each district paid. What a district gets back isn't traced, so this page estimates it: each year's recapture pool is shared out in proportion to each district's Foundation School Program state aid. Net flow = estimated share − recapture paid.

Recapture paid by Texas districts

FinalFY2026 near-final, FY2027 preliminary

TEA's recapture paid by district file. It matches the Chapter 49 payments in district books (General Fund, function 91) to within about 1% a year. FY2026–27 can't be split into a net flow yet: state-aid actuals end with FY2025.

The estimate treats recapture like any other money in the Foundation School Fund; in practice the Legislature sets total state aid, and recapture reduces how much general revenue it has to put in.

Sources and method

  • Revenue and spending FY2011–FY2025: Texas Education Agency, PEIMS district actual financial data (audited, every fund/function/object) for every independent school district. "All funds" means the General Fund, food service, federal and state/local grant funds, Debt Service and Capital Projects. Internal-service and fiduciary funds are left out so money isn't counted twice, and bond proceeds, refundings and transfers between funds aren't revenue. Charter schools (about 435,000 students) report separately and aren't included.
  • Federal categories follow TEA fund codes: 211/276 Title I; 224–226 IDEA-B; 266 (FY2020+), 277, 279, 281–285 COVID relief; 266 (FY2011) and 283–287 (FY2011–13) the 2009 stimulus and Education Jobs; General Fund objects 5931/5932 Medicaid. USDA child nutrition is federal revenue in the food-service fund (701, 240, 101 or summer-feeding 242).
  • School meals: Texas Department of Agriculture School Nutrition Programs meal reimbursement open data, program years 2015-16 to 2025-26, educational institutions only, summarized on data.texas.gov (October site rows and monthly totals per contracting entity). Entities are matched to TEA districts by county-district number, or by name before 2018-19. About 20 districts have no claims of their own: some aren't in the National School Lunch Program (Carroll, Highland Park) and some claim through a cooperative.
  • Regions are the 20 education service centers, taken from the meal claims. Similar size groups districts by FY2025 enrollment: under 500, 500–1,999, 2,000–9,999, 10,000–49,999 and 50,000+.
  • Enrollment: TEA Summarized PEIMS Actual Financial Data, fall survey enrollment. County outlines: U.S. Census Bureau, via plotly's county GeoJSON.
  • Inflation: CPI-U (not seasonally adjusted) from FRED, averaged July–June. Amounts are stored rounded to the nearest $1,000.
  • Fiscal years run July 1 to June 30 and are named for the year they end, so FY2025 is the 2024-25 school year. Rebuild with build/fetch.sh and build/build_data.py.
